To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that
we can classify the visual category of a stimulus from the pattern of activity in visual cortex, and we can do this with only 20 s of fMRI data at a time.

multivariate analysis of fMRI data can reveal distributed patterns of activity in human brain that are associated with the processing of specific categories of objects, and that such distributed patterns of activity can be used to classify individual trials on a near real time basis.
Multivariate statistical pattern recognition techniques can be used to classify distributed patterns of fMR signal in human visual cortex.
In summary, our research is concerned with
the development of new methods for the analysis of fMRI data that will allow the extraction of a much richer and more detailed set of information about the brain than has previously been possible.
developing and evaluating methods for using functional MRI (fMR) data to classify distributed patterns of brain activity associated with different categories of objects.
the development of a novel approach for analyzing brain activity patterns using multivariate statistical pattern analysis.
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that
fMRI is a powerful tool for the investigation of brain functions.
fMRI data are rich in information content that can be extracted by multivariate pattern recognition methods.

the use of pattern-recognition methods in fMRI data analysis allows the extraction of a great deal of information about the functional state of the brain that would not be possible with univariate analyses.

we can use the fMRI signal to classify visual stimuli with high accuracy, and we can do so in near real-time.

the human visual cortex is capable of encoding a great deal of visual information in the form of distributed patterns of activity, and that these patterns are stable enough that they can be reliably measured with fMRI.
the brain can be read in a similar fashion to how one can read a book.

fMRI data are rich with information that can be used to decode the content of a subject's visual percept on a trial-by-trial and subject-by-subject basis.

multivariate pattern analysis of fMRI data can reveal subtle differences in brain activity that are undetected using traditional (univariate) analyses, and that this approach has the potential to greatly increase the amount of information that can be extracted from fMRI studies of the human brain.
